Business Intelligence Basics: Designing Systems that Drive Decisions
Design a business intelligence system that turns scattered data into regular, trusted decisions for leaders and teams.

This course teaches BI as a system, not a tool. You will map decisions, assess data sources, write metric definitions, design a reporting structure and a governance plan, and learn to scope, price and lead BI work in African organisations.

What BI Is and Where It Fits

You learn what a business intelligence system is, the vocabulary professionals use, and how to judge how mature an organisation's BI already is. By the end you can describe any organisation's starting point and its next sensible step.
From data to decisions: what a BI system really is

Many businesses already have plenty of data. The POS terminal records every card payment, Paystack or Moniepoint keeps every transfer, the shop has a stock book, and the manager has a spreadsheet. Yet the owner still asks on Monday morning: "How much did we really sell last week, and what should I reorder?" and nobody can answer quickly with confidence. That gap is what **business intelligence (BI)** closes.

In this course, BI means **a deliberate, repeating system that gets the right information to the right decision-maker at the right time, so that a decision is made and acted on**. A dashboard is one part of it. Excel, SQL or Power BI are tools inside it. The system is the whole chain, plus the people and routines that keep it alive.

BI starts with the decisions people must make, then works back to the data.
The six links in the BI chain
The BI chain
Source systems
Collect and clean
One trusted store
Defined metrics
Reports and alerts
Decision and action
Information is only useful when every link works, from where data is born to what someone does with it.
**Source systems**: where data is born. POS, payment apps, accounting software, school or clinic software, WhatsApp order lists, paper registers.
**Collect and clean**: getting data out (exports, connectors, typing) and fixing spellings, duplicates and missing values. Professionals call this ETL: extract, transform, load.
**One trusted store**: a single place where the cleaned data lives. For a small business this can be one well-structured Google Sheet; for a bank it is a data warehouse.
**Defined metrics**: written definitions so that "sales" or "active customer" means the same thing in every report.
**Reports and alerts**: the delivery: a weekly one-page summary, a dashboard, a WhatsApp message when stock is low.
**Decision and action**: a named person looks at the information on a known day and decides something. Without this last link, the rest is decoration.

If any link breaks, the whole chain fails. A beautiful dashboard built on an export that nobody refreshes shows last month's numbers. A correct number delivered to the wrong person, or on the wrong day, changes nothing.
Start with decisions, not data

Beginners usually start by asking "What data do we have?" and then build charts of everything. BI designers start with a different question: **"What decisions does this business make again and again, and what would make them better?"** The tool for this is a **decision inventory**: a simple table listing each recurring decision, who makes it, how often, what information they need, where that information comes from today, and what is missing.
Worked example: a decision inventory for a frozen-food distributor
Funmi (for example) runs a frozen chicken and fish distribution business in Ibadan with two cold rooms. Each cold room manager counts stock by hand every Friday, which takes about 3 hours.
She lists five decisions she makes repeatedly: weekly reorder from suppliers, credit limits for retail customers, delivery van routes, monthly price review, and whether to open a third cold room.
For each decision she writes the owner and frequency. Reorder: Funmi, weekly. Credit limits: Funmi and her accountant, monthly. Routes: the logistics supervisor, daily.

She writes the information each one needs. Reorder needs stock on hand by product, sales in the last four weeks, and supplier lead time. Credit limits need each customer's purchases and how many days they take to pay.

She notes the current source and the gap. Stock comes from the Friday hand count (slow, no history kept). Customer payment days are not tracked at all: transfers sit in the bank app with no link to invoices.
She works out the cost of the manual count: 2 cold rooms x 3 hours x 52 weeks = 312 staff hours a year, and the result is thrown away after each reorder.
Funmi now sees that her two most valuable gaps are stock history and customer payment days. Her BI work should start there, not with a sales chart she already understands.

A tool is not a system

Buying Power BI or hiring someone who knows SQL does not create BI. Without agreed decisions, clean sources, written definitions and a routine for using the reports, the new tool simply produces faster confusion.

This course is about designing the whole system. Other WODDI Institute courses teach specific tools in depth, such as Excel dashboards, SQL and Power BI. Here you learn to decide what should be built, in what order, for whom, and how to keep it trustworthy. That is the work of a BI lead or BI consultant.

When you work with IT staff, software vendors or data engineers, they will use words that sound difficult. Each one names a simple idea. Learning them lets you lead the conversation, ask the right questions and check what you are being sold.

**OLTP** (online transaction processing) systems record day-to-day transactions: a sale, a payment, an enrolment. **OLAP** (online analytical processing) means storage and tools designed for analysis: adding up thousands of rows, comparing months, slicing by branch. BI almost always copies data out of OLTP systems into an analytical store, so reports do not slow down the till and history is kept even when the source system overwrites old values.
Moving data: ETL and ELT
**ETL**: extract data from the source, transform it (clean, rename, join, calculate), then load the clean result into the store.
**ELT**: extract and load the raw data first, then transform it inside the store. Common with cloud warehouses that have plenty of computing power.
Either way, the transform rules must be written down, because they decide what every number means.
Where data is kept
**Data warehouse**: a central, structured store of cleaned, integrated data from many sources, kept over time for reporting.
**Data mart**: a smaller slice of the warehouse for one department, for example finance or sales.
**Data lake**: a large store of raw files of many kinds (exports, logs, images), often kept before anyone has decided how to use them. Without discipline it becomes a "data swamp".

Ask any vendor which of these they are actually offering. A product described as a "data platform" might be a warehouse, a lake, a dashboard tool or all three, and the answer changes the cost, the skills needed and who will maintain it.
For a small business, the "warehouse" may honestly be one Google Sheet with a clean sales table and a clean customer table. The idea is the same: one trusted place, separate from the source apps.
Grain, facts and dimensions

The Kimball Group, whose dimensional modelling methods are widely used in BI, puts it simply: the grain "establishes exactly what a single fact table row represents". It must be declared before you choose anything else, and different grains should never be mixed in one table. **Facts** are the numbers you add up (quantity, amount). **Dimensions** are the things you slice by (date, branch, product, customer).
Worked example: choosing the grain for a supermarket's sales table
Ngozi (for example) is designing a sales table for a supermarket with 3 branches, about 400 products, and around 250 receipts per branch per day, each with about 4 items.
Option A grain: one row per product per branch per day. Maximum rows in a 30-day month: 3 x 400 x 30 = 36,000 rows (fewer in practice, because not every product sells every day).
Option B grain: one row per receipt line (one item on one receipt). Rows per day: 3 branches x 250 receipts x 4 lines = 3,000. Per 30-day month: 3,000 x 30 = 90,000 rows.
She checks the questions in the decision inventory. The owner wants to know which payment method customers use at different hours, and which products are bought together.
Option A cannot answer either question, because it has no receipt, no time and no payment method. Option B can.
She chooses Option B, the most detailed (atomic) grain, and writes the declaration at the top of the table: "One row = one item line on one receipt."

The table holds about 90,000 rows a month, easily handled by Power BI or a database, and it can answer the owner's real questions. Daily totals can always be added up from it, but receipt detail can never be recovered from daily totals.
Two more words you will hear

**Latency** or **refresh frequency** means how old the data is when someone sees it: real-time, hourly, daily or monthly. **Single source of truth** means one agreed store and one agreed definition for each key number. Ask about both in every BI conversation.

Before you recommend anything, you need to know where an organisation is starting from. A cooperative that keeps contributions in a notebook needs very different help from a bank with ten systems and a data team. A **maturity model** is a simple way to describe that starting point and agree on the next realistic step.

A 10-question maturity check

Score each question 0 (no), 1 (partly) or 2 (yes). The maximum is 20. Use the total as a guide, then confirm with what you see: 0 to 5 suggests level 1, 6 to 9 level 2, 10 to 13 level 3, 14 to 17 level 4, and 18 to 20 level 5.
Are the main transactions (sales, payments, enrolments, donations) recorded digitally?
Is there one agreed place where cleaned data for reporting is kept?
Are key metrics written down with a formula and an owner?
Do standard reports refresh on a schedule without someone rebuilding them?
Does the same number appear the same in every report?
Can managers get the information they need within a day of asking?
Are there routine checks for missing, duplicate or invalid records?
Is access to personal and financial data limited to the right people?
Are reports reviewed in a regular meeting where decisions are recorded?
Can the organisation name a decision that changed because of a report in the last three months?
Worked example: scoring a thrift and credit cooperative
Hauwa (for example) is the new administrator of a cooperative in Kaduna with about 600 members. Contributions are paid by bank transfer and recorded in Excel by two officers.

She scores the ten questions: 2 (contributions are digital), 1 (two separate Excel files), 0 (no written definitions), 0 (reports rebuilt each month), 0 (the two files often disagree), 1 (answers take about a week), 0 (no checks), 1 (files are shared on WhatsApp but only among officers), 1 (monthly executive meeting, no decision log), 0 (nobody can name a changed decision).
A score of 6 falls in the 6 to 9 band: level 2, spreadsheet reporting.
From the table, the next step is to agree definitions (for example, what makes a member "in good standing") and merge the two files into one trusted register.
The cooperative is at level 2. Hauwa recommends one shared register and five written definitions before anyone talks about dashboards.
Do not skip levels

A common and costly mistake is buying a dashboard tool for a level 1 or level 2 organisation. The dashboard looks impressive at the launch, then shows wrong or stale numbers, and leaders stop trusting data altogether. Fix the foundations first.
Where BI design work is found
Any organisation with several systems, several managers and recurring decisions needs BI thinking. In Nigeria and across Africa this includes:
**Distribution and retail**: FMCG distributors, pharmacies and supermarkets with several branches, POS terminals and stock to manage.
**Financial services**: banks, microfinance banks, cooperatives and fintechs tracking loans, repayments and customer activity.
**Education**: private schools and training centres tracking fees, enrolment, attendance and results.
**Health**: clinics, hospitals and diagnostic labs tracking patients, services, stock and claims.
**NGOs and programmes**: organisations that must report to donors on reach and results across several states or countries.
**Government agencies and associations**: registrations, revenue and service delivery records.

Roles you will see advertised include **BI analyst** (builds reports and answers questions), **BI developer** (builds data models and dashboards), **data engineer** (builds pipelines and warehouses), **analytics engineer** (turns raw data into clean, documented tables) and **BI lead or manager** (owns the strategy, priorities and governance). This course prepares you for the strategy and design side, which is often missing even when tool skills are present.

Local realities shape good design: expensive mobile data, unreliable power, many people working only on phones, and a lot of business happening on WhatsApp. A good BI design for a Nigerian SME may deliver a short PDF or image summary on WhatsApp each Monday rather than expect managers to open a heavy dashboard.

You turn decisions into a blueprint: a data source map, a metric dictionary, a prioritised reporting structure and a governance plan. These are the documents that make any BI tool produce numbers people trust and use.

BI design depends more on a few well-kept documents than on any single software product. You already know the first one, the **decision inventory**. This lesson adds two more: the **data source map** and the **metric dictionary**. Together they become the blueprint that any tool, from Google Sheets to Power BI, can then implement.

The data source map

A data source map lists every system that holds data needed by the decision inventory. For each system you record: what it records, who owns it, how data can be taken out (manual export, scheduled export, connector or API, or retyping), how often it changes, known quality problems, and whether it contains **personal data** such as names, phone numbers or health details.

To compare sources quickly, rate three things from 1 (poor) to 3 (good): **access** (how easy it is to get the data out), **quality** (how complete and correct it is) and **frequency** (how fresh it can be). The total, out of 9, shows which sources are ready to use now and which need work first.
Worked example: mapping a private school's data sources
Blessing (for example) is designing BI for a private secondary school in Abuja. The proprietor's top decisions are fee follow-up, staffing per class and which students need academic support.

She finds four sources: fee payments (bank statements and the Paystack dashboard export), the student register (an Excel file kept by the admin officer), results (a school management app that exports CSV) and attendance (paper registers in each class).
Fee payments: access 3 (CSV export), quality 2 (some parents pay with a sibling's name as reference), frequency 3 (daily). Total 8.
Student register: access 3, quality 2 (duplicate names after transfers), frequency 2 (updated each term). Total 7.
Results app: access 2 (export only by the vice principal), quality 3, frequency 1 (once a term). Total 6.
Attendance registers: access 1 (paper), quality 2, frequency 1 (would need weekly typing). Total 4.
Fees and the student register (8 and 7) are ready for a first report. Attendance (4) needs a simple digital register before it can feed any decision, so Blessing puts it in phase two.
The metric dictionary

A **metric dictionary** is the single written definition of every key number. Without it, the bursar, the principal and the proprietor will each calculate "fees collected" slightly differently, and the first meeting with the new report becomes an argument. Each entry has:
**Name** and plain-language meaning
**Formula**, with exactly which records are included and excluded
**Source** and the field names used
**Owner**: the one person who approves any change to the definition
**Refresh**: how often it updates, and when
**Target or threshold**, if any, and who set it
Field
Entry: Fee collection rate
Meaning
Share of this term's billed fees that has been received
Formula
Fees received for the term divided by fees billed for the term, x 100
Includes
Tuition and compulsory levies billed this term
Excludes
Students on full scholarship; optional items such as excursions
Source
Billing sheet (billed), bank and Paystack exports matched to student ID (received)
Bursar

Every Monday by 10 am
Example

Notice the exclusions. If scholarship students are left in the billed figure, the rate looks worse than it really is, and the proprietor may chase the wrong families. A definition is only complete when it says what is left out.

Write a one-page reporting structure for an organisation

A decision inventory for even a small organisation can list 20 or more decisions. You cannot serve them all at once. Professional BI work moves in a clear sequence: **discover, prioritise, design the reporting structure, build the smallest useful version, launch it into a real meeting, then measure use and improve**. This lesson covers the middle steps: prioritising and designing.
A person moving task cards across a board
Prioritising decisions turns a long wish list into a short, ordered build plan.
Step 1: score value and feasibility

For each decision, score two things from 1 to 5. **Value**: how much money, time or risk depends on getting it right. **Feasibility**: how ready the data is (use your source map scores) and how easy the report is to build. Multiply the two for a priority score out of 25.
Decision priority matrix
Major projects: plan carefully
Quick wins: do first
Avoid for now
Fill-ins: do when convenient
Feasibility (higher to the right)
Value (higher at the top)
High-value, high-feasibility decisions come first; high-value but low-feasibility ones need data work before reports.
Worked example: prioritising a beverage distributor's decisions
Chidi (for example) leads BI for a soft drinks distributor in Onitsha with three depots and twelve sales reps. Discovery produced six decisions.
Weekly reorder per depot: value 5, feasibility 4, score 5 x 4 = 20.
Monthly sales rep incentives: value 4, feasibility 4, score 16.
Retailer credit limits: value 5, feasibility 3, score 15.
Product price changes: value 4, feasibility 2, score 8.
Delivery route planning: value 3, feasibility 2, score 6.
Opening a fourth depot: value 5, feasibility 1, score 5 (once a year, needs data the company does not yet collect).

Chidi builds for reorder (20), incentives (16) and credit limits (15) first. The fourth depot decision is valuable but not feasible yet, so he adds "start recording retailer locations" to the data work plan instead.
Step 2: design the reporting tiers

Different people need different views at different speeds. A strong reporting structure has three tiers. Each tier answers different questions, so they should not be squeezed into one crowded dashboard.

Notice that operational reports are mostly **lists of things to act on**, not charts. A supervisor needs "these 7 retailers are more than 30 days overdue, call them today", not a pie chart of overdue balances.
Step 3: the rhythm of business
Each report should be tied to a fixed moment when someone uses it. Write a simple calendar, sometimes called the **rhythm of business**:
Daily, 8 am: depot supervisors receive the low-stock and overdue-retailer lists.
Monday, 10 am: weekly sales meeting uses the tactical dashboard, refreshed by 9 am.
First Thursday of the month: management meeting reviews the strategic page and records decisions.
Quarterly: board pack includes the strategic page with quarter-on-quarter trends.
When a report has no meeting or moment attached to it, it will soon stop being read. If nobody can name the meeting, question whether the report should exist.
Sketch each page before building

Before anyone opens a BI tool, sketch each report on paper or in a slide: a **wireframe**. It is far cheaper to move boxes on paper than to rebuild a finished dashboard. Show the sketch to the person who will use the page and ask: "Which decision does this help you make, and is anything missing or unnecessary?"
Put the most important number for the decision at the top left, where the eye lands first.
Show every headline number with a comparison: against target, last period or the same period last year. A number alone cannot tell the reader whether to worry.
Print the last refresh date and time on every page, so nobody decides on stale data without knowing it.
Link or footnote each metric to its metric dictionary definition.
Keep a page readable on a phone screen if managers mainly use phones: few numbers, large text, short lists.
Step 4: build small, launch into a real meeting
Build the first release for the top two or three decisions only, often in two to four weeks.
Test the numbers with the metric owners before anyone else sees them.
Launch by using the report live in its real meeting, not with a separate presentation.
Write down which decisions were made using it.
Collect feedback after the first three or four uses, then plan the next release.
The everything dashboard
Putting every metric for every audience on one page is the most common design failure. It loads slowly on phones, confuses readers and serves nobody well. Three focused tiers beat one crowded screen.

Building trust: data quality checks, metric governance and data protection
Measure data quality using six recognised dimensions
Set up metric ownership, change control and a certified-report label
Apply data protection practices in line with Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023
Write a short governance plan that keeps a BI system trustworthy over time

A BI system lives or dies on trust. The first time a manager finds a wrong number in a report, they start keeping their own spreadsheet again. **Data quality** keeps the numbers right, **governance** keeps the definitions stable, and **data protection** keeps people's information safe. All three must be designed, not hoped for.
A person checking documents marked as reviewed
Regular checks and clear ownership are what make people trust the numbers.
Six dimensions of data quality
The UK Government Data Quality Framework, a widely used public reference, names six core dimensions. Each one becomes a simple check you can run every time data is refreshed.
Dimension
Example check
Completeness
Records and values are present
Share of member records with a phone number
Uniqueness
No duplicate records
Count of member IDs that appear more than once
Consistency
Values do not contradict each other
Same customer has the same branch in sales and in the customer list
Timeliness
Data is up to date for the period it represents
Last refresh date shown on every report
Validity
Values are in the expected range and format
Dates are real dates; amounts are not negative
Accuracy
Data matches reality
Monthly total matches the bank statement
Worked example: scoring a cooperative's member register
Following the maturity check, Hauwa (for example) merges the cooperative's two Excel files into one register of 1,250 member records and checks it before building any report.
Completeness: 75 records have no phone number. Complete records: 1,250 - 75 = 1,175. Score: 1,175 / 1,250 x 100 = 94%.
Uniqueness: 30 records repeat a member ID already in the list. Unique records: 1,250 - 30 = 1,220. Score: 1,220 / 1,250 x 100 = 97.6%.
Validity: 18 records have a joining date in the future or in the wrong format. Valid: 1,232 / 1,250 x 100 = 98.56%, about 98.6%.
Accuracy: total contributions in the register for June are ₦8,460,000; the bank statement shows ₦8,535,000. Difference: ₦75,000, which she traces to three transfers recorded under the wrong month.
She fixes the problems at the source (the officers' entry form now requires a phone number and checks the date) instead of patching the report.
Hauwa removes the 30 duplicates, corrects the three transfers and starts showing the four scores at the bottom of every monthly report, so officers can see quality improve.
The data quality cycle
Define the rule
Measure the score
Fix at the source
Monitor each refresh
Review rules quarterly
Quality is a routine, not a one-time clean-up: problems fixed only in the report will come back next month.
Metric governance
Governance means agreed rules about who decides what. Keep it light but real:
**One owner per metric.** Only the owner can approve a change to its definition in the metric dictionary.
**Change log.** Every change records the date, what changed, why, and who approved it, so last year's numbers can still be explained.
**Certified versus exploratory.** Mark reports built from the trusted store and dictionary as certified. Anything else is exploratory and must not be quoted in board papers.
**A data steward.** One person, often part-time, runs the quality checks and keeps the dictionary up to date.
**Quarterly review.** Retire reports nobody uses and review definitions that cause arguments.
One word, three meanings

In many organisations "active member" or "active customer" means something different to each manager: paid this month, paid in the last three months, or simply not closed. Pick one, write it in the dictionary with an owner, and show the definition on the report itself.
Protecting personal data

BI brings personal data from many systems into one place, which raises the risk if something goes wrong. In Nigeria, the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023** set up the **Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)**, which enforces data protection rules. Read the Act and NDPC guidance for any organisation you advise, and involve the organisation's legal adviser or data protection officer where one exists. Practical design habits:
Collect and load only the personal fields a decision really needs.
Show totals and counts in reports; keep names and phone numbers only in operational lists for staff who must act on them.
Give access by role: a branch manager sees her branch, not every customer in the company.
Do not share raw exports in WhatsApp groups or personal email. Share a link with access control, or a summary without personal details.
Use strong, unique passwords and two-step verification on every BI and source account, and remove access the day someone leaves.
Keep health, salary and similar sensitive data out of general dashboards entirely.
Scam and leak warning

Customer lists with phone numbers and balances are valuable to fraudsters. Never send them to someone who claims, by phone or chat, to be from a bank, regulator or "IT support". Confirm through a known official contact first.
Measure completeness, uniqueness, consistency, timeliness, validity and accuracy
Fix data problems at the source, then monitor them every refresh
Every metric has one owner, and every definition change is logged
Mark certified reports so leaders know which numbers to quote
Load only the personal data you need, restrict access by role, and never share raw exports casually

Leading BI Work: Discovery, Pricing, Adoption and Portfolio

You learn to run discovery with decision-makers, price and scope a BI strategy engagement, and lead the adoption that makes the system worth its cost. You finish with a roadmap and a portfolio case study.
Discovery with decision-makers: interviews, stakeholder lists and the current-state report
Plan a one-week BI discovery with the right people in the right order
Ask interview questions that uncover decisions, not just data wishes
Turn interview notes into decision inventory entries
Write and present a short current-state report

Discovery is where BI projects are won or lost. If you only talk to the IT officer about systems, you will design reports about data. If you talk to the people who make decisions, you will design reports that change what they do. Good discovery is short, structured and focused on **decisions, pain and evidence**.
Two people in a structured interview conversation
Discovery interviews focus on the decisions people make and what slows them down.
Who to talk to
**The sponsor**: the person paying for the work or championing it, often the owner, CEO or executive director. Agree the goal and budget with them first.
**Decision-makers**: the people in the decision inventory, from the owner to branch managers.
**Data keepers**: whoever enters, exports or controls the data in each source system.
**Report makers**: whoever builds the current reports by hand. They know where every problem hides.
**Report readers outside**: if donors, regulators or a board receive reports, find out exactly what they require.
A one-week discovery
Day 1: sponsor kick-off
Days 2 to 3: interviews
Day 4: source review
Day 5: findings playback
A short, fixed timetable keeps discovery focused and shows the client progress quickly.
Questions that reveal decisions
Avoid asking "What reports do you want?" People will list every chart they have ever seen. Ask about their work instead.
Area
Questions
Decisions
What decisions do you make every week or month? Which one costs the most when it goes wrong?
Current information
What do you look at before you decide? Where does it come from? How old is it by the time you see it?
Pain
Tell me about the last time the numbers were wrong or late. What happened?
Effort
Who prepares the report you use? How many hours does it take each time?
Data
Which systems hold this information? Who can export it? Is any of it on paper?
Success
If this worked perfectly in six months, what would you be doing differently?

Listen for numbers and stories. "The quarterly donor report takes my team two days per state" is far more useful than "reporting is stressful". Write down exact phrases; they will go into your report and help the sponsor recognise their own organisation.
Worked example: discovery for an NGO skills programme
Amina (for example) runs discovery for an NGO that trains young women in tailoring and digital skills in 4 states and reports quarterly to two donors.

The programme director says her biggest decision is where to move trainers and funds each quarter. Today she decides from memory and phone calls, because the donor report arrives a month after the quarter ends.

Each of the 4 state coordinators spends about 2 days per quarter compiling attendance and completion figures from paper and Google Forms. That is 4 x 2 = 8 person-days per quarter, or 8 x 4 = 32 person-days a year.
The two donors define "completion" differently: one counts 80% attendance, the other requires passing a final assessment. Coordinators keep two separate tallies.

Amina writes three decision inventory entries: quarterly reallocation of trainers and funds (director), monthly follow-up of at-risk trainees (state coordinators), quarterly donor reporting (M&E officer).
She adds a metric dictionary note: two completion definitions are needed, each owned by the M&E officer and labelled by donor.

The discovery shows that a monthly state-by-state view of enrolment, attendance and both completion measures would serve the director's decision and cut most of the 32 person-days a year of manual compiling.

Many interviews will happen by phone, WhatsApp call or Zoom, especially across states. Ask permission before recording, keep each call to 30 to 45 minutes, and type up your notes the same day while details are fresh. Send each person a three-line summary of what you heard so they can correct anything you misunderstood.
The current-state report
End discovery with a short report, five to eight pages at most, and present it in a playback meeting. Structure:
**Goal**: the sponsor's goal in one or two sentences, in their words.
**Decisions**: the decision inventory, ranked by value and feasibility.
**Current state**: maturity score, the source map with ratings, and the main pain points with real examples and hours spent.
**Key issues**: conflicting definitions, quality problems, access or privacy risks.
**Recommendation**: the first release (two or three decisions), what data work is needed first, and the proposed next phase.
**Questions still open** and who will answer them.
Confirm before you build
In the playback meeting, ask the sponsor to confirm the top three decisions in writing, for example by replying to your summary email. This agreement protects you later when new requests appear.
Handle access carefully

During discovery, ask to see sample exports or screens, not passwords. If you must log into a system, ask the owner to create a separate account for you with read-only access, and ask for it to be removed when the project ends.
Talk first to the sponsor, then decision-makers, data keepers and report makers
Ask about decisions, pain, effort and success, not about wished-for charts
Capture real numbers such as hours spent and days of delay
End with a short current-state report and get written agreement on priorities
Request read-only accounts, never other people's passwords

Pricing a BI strategy engagement and controlling scope
Choose between fixed-fee, phased and retainer pricing for BI work
Estimate an engagement from task-level days and add contingency
Write the scope, assumptions and exclusions sections of a proposal
Handle new requests with a simple change request process

BI strategy work is senior work. You are helping leaders decide how information will flow through their organisation for years. Price it on the effort and expertise involved, write down exactly what is included, and protect both sides with a clear agreement.
A signed contract document with a pen
A written scope and payment schedule protect both you and the client.
Three common pricing models
Model
What it covers
Good when
Risk
Fixed fee, strategy and roadmap
Discovery, source map, metric dictionary, reporting design, roadmap
Scope is clear after a short first conversation
Scope creep if exclusions are not written
Phased implementation
Separate fee per phase: foundations, first release, next release
Large or uncertain projects
Client may stop after phase one
Monthly retainer
A fixed number of days each month for governance, quality checks, new reports, training
After launch, to keep the system healthy
Unused days cause disputes unless rules are clear
Estimating from tasks

Do not guess a single total. List the tasks, estimate the days for each, multiply by your day rate, then add contingency for the unknowns. Your day rate depends on your experience, the client's size and your market. The rate below is only an example to show the method, not a market price.
Worked example: a strategy engagement for a pharmacy chain
Kemi (for example) is quoting a BI strategy and roadmap for a pharmacy chain with five branches in Lagos. She uses an example day rate of ₦75,000.

Discovery interviews and site visits: 4 days. Source assessment and data source map: 3 days. Metric dictionary for 15 metrics: 3 days. Reporting structure and wireframes: 2 days. Roadmap, governance plan and final presentation: 2 days.
Total effort: 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 14 days.
Contingency of 15% for unknown data problems: ₦1,050,000 x 0.15 = ₦157,500.
Payment schedule 40% / 40% / 20%: ₦483,000 at signing, ₦483,000 after the current-state report, ₦241,500 after the final presentation.
Kemi's proposal shows the task list and days, so the client sees what they are paying for. A follow-on retainer of 2 days a month would be 2 x ₦75,000 = ₦150,000 a month at the same example rate.
Scope: in and out
Writing the scope
In scope
Out of scope
Interviews with up to 8 people
Source map for 5 named systems
Metric dictionary, up to 15 metrics
Reporting design and roadmap
Building dashboards in a tool
Fixing data inside source systems
Staff training beyond one session
New branches added mid-project
Listing what is excluded is as important as listing what is included; it is where most disputes start.

A proposal should also list **assumptions**: what the client must provide and by when. For example: "The client will provide exports from the POS and accounting system within 5 working days of signing" and "Interviews will be scheduled within the first two weeks." If an assumption fails, the timeline or fee can be reviewed.
What the proposal contains
**Background**: the client's goal in their words, from discovery.
**Deliverables**: each document or report, described so that both sides can tell when it is finished.
**Approach and timeline**: the phases, the meetings and the dates.
**Scope, exclusions and assumptions**, as above.
**Fee and payment schedule**, with what triggers each payment.
**Confidentiality and data handling**: how you will store, use and delete the client's data at the end.

For retainers, write how unused days are treated (for example, they do not roll over, or they roll over for one month only), how requests are submitted, and how quickly you respond. Send a short monthly note listing the days used and the work done, so the client sees the value of the retainer every month.
Handling new requests
Thank the person and write the request down exactly.
Check it against the written scope. If it is already included, schedule it.
If it is new, estimate the extra days and the effect on the deadline.
Send a short change request: what, why, days, cost, new date.
Start only after the sponsor approves it in writing, even by email or a WhatsApp message you keep.
Protect the money

Issue a proper invoice with your business name and bank details, and receive payment by traceable bank transfer. Confirm that money has actually arrived in your own bank app before releasing work. Payment screenshots and "debit alerts" forwarded by someone else can be faked. If you operate as a business, register it with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) so your invoices and contracts carry a registered name.
Price the value, explain the effort

When a client says the fee is high, go back to the discovery numbers. If the organisation spends 32 person-days a year compiling one report, or loses money on late reorders every month, show how the design addresses that. Do not cut days without cutting scope.
Use fixed fee for clear strategy work, phases for big projects, retainers after launch

Write scope, exclusions and client assumptions in the proposal
New requests go through a written change request before work starts

Leading adoption, measuring impact and building your BI portfolio
Plan training and routines that get BI reports used in real decisions
Measure adoption and impact with simple, honest metrics
Write a now, next, later BI roadmap
Assemble a BI strategy case study for your portfolio

A BI system is only finished when people use it to decide. Many technically good projects fail quietly: the dashboard launches, usage fades within weeks, and managers return to their private spreadsheets. As the BI lead, adoption is your job, not an afterthought.
A team working together around shared screens
Adoption happens in meetings and routines, not at the launch event.
What drives adoption
**Use it in the meeting.** The sponsor opens the report at the start of the weekly or monthly meeting and asks questions from it. When the leader uses it, others follow.
**Retire the old reports.** If the old manual report still arrives, people will keep using it. Agree a date to stop it.
**Train by role, briefly.** A 30-minute session per role, using their own data and their own decisions, works better than a long general training.
**Choose champions.** One person in each branch or department who is comfortable with the report and helps colleagues.
**Make feedback easy.** A simple form or WhatsApp number for "this number looks wrong" reports, with a promise to reply within two working days.
Measuring adoption and impact
Track a few honest measures for the first three months after launch:
Measure
How to calculate
Why it matters
Active user rate
Intended users who opened the report in the period, divided by all intended users
Shows whether people look at it
Decisions logged
Number of decisions recorded in meeting notes that used the report
Shows whether it changes what people do
Time saved
Hours spent compiling reports before, minus hours after
Shows the efficiency gain
Quality issues
Problems reported and the share fixed within the promised time
Shows whether trust is being protected
Worked example: an eight-week adoption review
Chidi (for example) reviews the beverage distributor's BI system eight weeks after launch. Twenty managers and supervisors were meant to use the reports.
Active users: 14 of 20 opened the weekly report at least once a week. Rate: 14 / 20 x 100 = 70%.
He checks who is missing: all 6 non-users work at the depot with the weakest mobile network. He arranges a PDF summary on WhatsApp for them each Monday.

Time saved: before, 2 staff spent 3 days each per month compiling reports, 2 x 3 = 6 person-days. Now 1 person spends 1 day checking the refresh. Saving: 6 - 1 = 5 person-days a month, or 5 x 12 = 60 person-days a year.
Decisions logged: the meeting notes show 9 reorder decisions and 3 credit limit changes made using the reports.
Quality: 7 issues reported, 6 fixed within two working days. Rate: 6 / 7 x 100 = about 86%.
Chidi reports to the owner with numbers, not impressions, and his next action is aimed at the real cause of low use: network access at one depot.
The BI roadmap: now, next, later
A three-horizon BI roadmap
Now: top 3 decisions
Next: fix weak sources
Later: forecasting and alerts
A roadmap in three horizons shows leaders the path without promising exact dates for uncertain work.

**Now** (the current quarter) covers the first release and governance basics. **Next** covers the sources and decisions that needed data work, such as digitising attendance or recording retailer locations. **Later** covers advanced work such as forecasting, which only makes sense once history is clean. Review the roadmap with the sponsor every quarter.
Your BI portfolio

Tool skills are shown by dashboards. BI strategy skills are shown by **the documents that come before the dashboard**. Build one strong case study, for a real organisation with permission, or for a realistic invented one clearly labelled as a practice case.
**Context**: the organisation type, size and goal, without confidential details.
**Decision inventory**: ranked by value and feasibility.
**Maturity score and data source map** with ratings.
**Metric dictionary**: at least five complete entries.
**Reporting structure**: three tiers and the rhythm of business.
**Governance plan**: quality checks, owners, data protection rules.
**Results or expected impact**: adoption and time-saved numbers if real, clearly marked estimates if not.
Protect client data in your portfolio

Remove names, phone numbers, account details and real financial figures unless the client agrees in writing. Replace them with realistic sample values and say so. A portfolio that leaks client data will cost you more work than it wins.

Paths after this course differ by where you want to work. Inside an organisation, the natural step is from analyst or report builder to BI lead, owning priorities and governance. As a consultant, the strategy pack from your capstone becomes your first offer to clients. Either way, keep building tool depth alongside strategy, so you can judge what your designs will cost to build.

When you present your case study to a future client or employer, lead with the decision you improved and the time or money it affected, then show the documents. This is what separates a BI lead from someone who only builds charts.

This is the video for Module 1 of Business Intelligence Basics: what BI is and where it fits.
Why this matters
Plenty of data, no quick answers
The POS, payment apps and stock book all hold data
Yet nobody can answer Monday's questions
BI closes that gap
Right information, right person, right time
Many businesses already have plenty of data. The POS terminal records card payments, Paystack or Moniepoint keeps every transfer, and the shop has a stock book.
Yet on Monday morning the owner asks, how much did we really sell last week, and what should I reorder? And nobody can answer quickly with confidence.
That gap is what business intelligence, or BI, closes.
In this course, BI means a repeating system that gets the right information to the right decision-maker at the right time, so a decision is made and acted on.
The whole system
If any link breaks, the whole chain fails.
Source systems: where data is born
Collect and clean, called ETL
Defined metrics, written down
Decision and action by a named person
First, source systems, where data is born: the POS, payment apps, accounting software, WhatsApp order lists, even paper registers.
Next, collect and clean: getting data out and fixing spellings, duplicates and gaps. Professionals call this ETL, which means extract, transform, load.
Then one trusted store. For a small business, that can be one well-structured Google Sheet.
Then defined metrics, so that sales means the same thing in every report.
Then the reports and alerts themselves, such as a weekly one-page summary, or a WhatsApp message when stock is low.
And last, a named person looks at the information on a known day and decides something. Without this link, the rest is decoration.
Worked example
Funmi's decision inventory
List decisions made again and again
Write the owner and how often
Write the information each one needs
Note today's source and the gap
Count the cost of the manual way
BI designers do not start with what data do we have. They ask, what decisions does this business make again and again? The tool is a decision inventory.
For example, Funmi runs a frozen chicken and fish business in Ibadan with two cold rooms.
She lists five repeated decisions, such as the weekly reorder, customer credit limits and delivery van routes.
For each, she writes the owner and how often. The reorder is hers, weekly.
The reorder needs stock by product, sales in the last four weeks, and supplier lead time.
Stock comes from a Friday hand count with no history kept. And customer payment days are not tracked at all.
The hand count takes 2 cold rooms times 3 hours times 52 weeks. That is 312 staff hours a year, thrown away after each reorder. So her BI work starts with stock history and payment days.
Key words
Running the business vs answering questions
OLTP
OLAP
OLTP systems run the business. They record each sale, payment or enrolment, and must be fast.
OLAP means storage built for analysis: adding thousands of rows and comparing months. BI copies data into a separate store, so reports do not slow down the till and history is kept.
Where are they now?
1. Scattered: notebooks, phones, heads
2. Spreadsheet reporting by hand
3. Centralised: one trusted store
4. Managed: owners, checks, access rules
5. Decision-driven: reports used in meetings
Before you recommend anything, find the starting point. At level 1, data is scattered in notebooks, phones and people's heads.
At level 2, monthly reports are built by hand from exports, and numbers often disagree.
At level 3, one trusted store exists, and standard reports refresh on schedule.
At level 4, metrics have owners, quality checks and access rules.
At level 5, reports are used in fixed review meetings, and actions are tracked.
Scoring a cooperative
Fix the foundations before you buy a dashboard tool.
Score 10 questions: 0 no, 1 partly, 2 yes
Hauwa's total: 6
6 to 9 means level 2
Next step: definitions and one register
A 10-question check helps. Score each question 0 for no, 1 for partly, or 2 for yes. The maximum is 20.
For example, Hauwa runs a cooperative in Kaduna with about 600 members. Contributions are recorded in two Excel files that often disagree. Her total is 6.
A score of 6 to 9 means level 2, spreadsheet reporting.
So her next step is written definitions and one trusted register, not a dashboard. Buying a dashboard tool too early shows wrong numbers, and leaders stop trusting data altogether.
Key points
Remember
BI is a repeating system, not a tool
Every link must work, up to the action
Start with a decision inventory
Run reports on a separate store
Know the maturity level before you build
To remember. BI is a repeating system, not a tool, and every link must work, right up to the action.
Start with a decision inventory, keep reporting separate from the till, and know the maturity level before you build.

The BI blueprint: sources, definitions, tiers and trust
The BI blueprint: sources, definitions, tiers and trust.
This is the video for Module 2 of Business Intelligence Basics: designing the BI system.
Why this matters
Documents before dashboards
A data source map
A metric dictionary
A reporting structure people use
Checks that keep numbers trusted
BI design depends more on a few well-kept documents than on any single software product. Together they make a blueprint that any tool, from Google Sheets to Power BI, can build.
A data source map shows where the data lives.
A metric dictionary says what each number means.
A reporting structure gets the right view to the right person.
And quality checks keep people trusting the numbers.
Rate each source out of 9
Access: how easy to get the data out
Quality: how complete and correct
Frequency: how fresh it can be
Fee payments: 8, ready now
Paper attendance: 4, phase two
For every source system, rate three things from 1, poor, to 3, good.
Access, how easy it is to get the data out.
Quality, how complete and correct it is.
And frequency, how fresh it can be.
For example, Blessing designs BI for a private school in Abuja. Fee payments come as a daily CSV export, so they score 8 out of 9 and are ready for a first report.
Paper attendance registers score only 4. They need a simple digital register first, so she puts them in phase two.
Defining the fee collection rate
For example, the school's bursar owns the fee collection rate, refreshed every Monday by 10 am.
Fees billed this term
Fees received this term
Excludes full-scholarship students.
A metric dictionary is the single written definition of every key number. Each entry has a meaning, a formula, a source, one owner, and a refresh time.
Here, the owner is the bursar, and it refreshes every Monday by 10 am.
The school billed 48,600,000 naira this term.
It received 39,852,000 naira. Received divided by billed, times 100, is 82%.
Notice the exclusions. If scholarship students stay in the billed figure, the rate looks worse, and the proprietor may chase the wrong families.
Prioritise
Score value times feasibility
Build the highest scores first.
Value 1 to 5: money, time or risk at stake
Feasibility 1 to 5: data ready, easy to build
Weekly reorder: 5 x 4 = 20
Fourth depot: 5 x 1 = 5, data work first
You cannot serve every decision at once. Score each one for value from 1 to 5: how much money, time or risk depends on it.
Then score feasibility from 1 to 5: how ready the data is. Multiply the two for a score out of 25.
For example, Chidi leads BI for a soft drinks distributor in Onitsha. The weekly reorder scores 5 times 4, which is 20.
Opening a fourth depot is valuable, but the data is not collected yet, so it scores 5. Instead of a report, he adds start recording retailer locations to the data work plan.
Reporting tiers
Three tiers, not one crowded page
Owner or board, monthly or quarterly. 5 to 8 headline metrics against targets, on one page.
Branch and department managers, weekly. Breakdowns by branch, product or rep: what changed and why.
Supervisors, daily. Lists to act on: low stock, overdue payers, today's deliveries.
Different people need different views. The strategic tier serves the owner or board, monthly or quarterly, with 5 to 8 headline numbers against targets.
The tactical tier serves managers weekly, with breakdowns that show what changed and why.
The operational tier serves supervisors daily, with lists, not charts. These 7 retailers are more than 30 days overdue, call them today.
And tie every report to a fixed meeting. If nobody can name the meeting, question whether the report should exist.
Data quality
Six checks on every refresh
Completeness: values are present
Uniqueness: no duplicates
Consistency: no contradictions
Timeliness: refresh date on every report
Validity: right range and format
Accuracy: matches the bank statement
The first wrong number sends managers back to their private spreadsheets. So check six things every time data refreshes: completeness, uniqueness, consistency, timeliness, validity and accuracy.
For example, Hauwa finds 30 duplicate member IDs in her register of 1,250 records. She fixes problems at the source, not in the report, so they do not come back next month.
Protect people's data
Data protection habits
Never send customer lists to someone who just calls or chats.
Load only the personal fields a decision needs
Show totals; names only in action lists
Give access by role
No raw exports in WhatsApp groups
Strong passwords and two-step verification

BI brings personal data into one place, which raises the risk. In Nigeria, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 set up the NDPC to enforce data protection rules. Load only the personal fields a decision really needs.
Show totals in reports, and keep names and phone numbers only in lists for staff who must act on them.
A branch manager sees her branch, not every customer.
Do not share raw exports in WhatsApp groups or personal email.

Use strong passwords and two-step verification, and remove access the day someone leaves. Customer lists are valuable to fraudsters, so confirm anyone claiming to be a bank or IT support through a known official contact first.
Key points
Remember
Rate sources on access, quality, frequency
Every metric: formula, exclusions, one owner
Value times feasibility sets the order
Three tiers, each tied to a meeting
Fix quality at the source; protect personal data
To remember. Rate your sources. Write every metric with its exclusions and one owner. Build the highest scores first.
Use three tiers tied to meetings, fix quality at the source, and protect personal data.

Leading BI work: discover, price, and get it used.
This is the video for Module 3 of Business Intelligence Basics: leading BI work.
Why this matters
Where BI projects are won or lost
Discovery with the people who decide
A clear price and a written scope
Adoption: people using it to decide
A portfolio that shows your design work
Discovery is where BI projects are won or lost. Talk only to the IT officer, and you design reports about data. Talk to the people who decide, and you design reports that change what they do.
Then you price the work honestly and write down exactly what is included.
A BI system is only finished when people use it to decide.
And your portfolio shows the design documents behind the dashboard.
Discovery questions
Ask about work, not wished-for charts
Avoid
What reports do you want?
Reporting is stressful
Ask instead
Which decision costs most when wrong?
When were the numbers last wrong?
How many hours does the report take?
What would you do differently?
Avoid asking, what reports do you want? People will list every chart they have ever seen.
Ask about their work. Which decision costs the most when it goes wrong? Tell me about the last time the numbers were late. How many hours does the report take?
Listen for numbers and stories, and write down their exact phrases.
Worked example
Amina's NGO discovery
Director moves trainers from memory
4 coordinators x 2 days = 8 per quarter
32 person-days a year compiling
Two donors define completion differently

For example, Amina runs discovery for an NGO training young women in 4 states. The director decides where to move trainers and funds from memory and phone calls, because the donor report comes a month late.
Each of the 4 state coordinators spends about 2 days a quarter compiling figures. That is 8 person-days a quarter.
Or 32 person-days a year.
And the two donors define completion differently, so the dictionary needs two labelled definitions. A monthly state-by-state view would serve the director and cut most of that compiling.
End discovery with a short report, and get the sponsor to confirm the top three decisions in writing.
Pricing from tasks
Kemi's quote for a pharmacy chain
For example, Kemi quotes a BI strategy for a pharmacy chain with five branches in Lagos.
Base fee: 14 days x 75,000
Contingency, 15%
75,000 is an example day rate only.
Do not guess a single total. List the tasks, estimate days, multiply by your day rate, and add contingency.
For example, Kemi's tasks add up to 14 days. Her day rate of 75,000 naira is only an example to show the method.
14 days at 75,000 naira gives a base fee of 1,050,000 naira.
She adds 15% for unknown data problems, which is 157,500 naira.
Her quote is 1,207,500 naira, paid 40%, 40% and 20% at agreed points. The client can see exactly what they are paying for.
Scope and payment
Confirm money in your own bank app before releasing work.
Write the request down exactly
Check it against the written scope
If new, estimate extra days and the new date
Send a short change request
Start only after written approval
Write scope, exclusions and client assumptions into the proposal. When a new request comes, thank the person and write it down exactly.
Check it against the written scope. If it is included, schedule it.
Send a short change request: what, why, days, cost and new date.
Start only after the sponsor approves it in writing.
Issue a proper invoice, and confirm that money has really arrived in your own bank app. Screenshots and forwarded debit alerts can be faked.
Adoption
What gets reports used
The leader uses it in the meeting
Retire the old reports on a set date
30-minute training per role
A champion in each branch
Easy feedback, reply in two working days
Many good projects fail quietly, and managers return to their private spreadsheets. So the sponsor opens the report at the start of the meeting and asks questions from it.
Agree a date to stop the old manual report.
Train each role briefly, using their own data and decisions.
Choose one champion in each branch or department.
And make it easy to say this number looks wrong, with a reply within two working days.
Chidi's eight-week review
14 of 20 opened the report weekly. All 6 non-users work at the depot with the weakest network.
From 6 person-days a month to 1. That is 60 person-days a year.
9 reorder decisions and 3 credit limit changes made using the reports.

For example, Chidi reviews his distributor's system eight weeks after launch. 14 of 20 managers used it, which is 70%. All 6 non-users work at the depot with the weakest mobile network, so he sends them a PDF summary on WhatsApp each Monday.
Compiling used to take 6 person-days a month. Now it takes 1, saving 60 person-days a year.
And the meeting notes show 9 reorder decisions and 3 credit limit changes made with the reports. He reports with numbers, not impressions.
Key points
Remember
Ask about decisions, pain, effort and success
Price task by task, plus contingency
Write scope, exclusions and assumptions
Leaders use reports; old reports retire
Roadmap: now, next, later
To remember. Ask about decisions and pain. Price task by task, and write down what is out of scope.
Lead adoption by using reports in meetings, and show leaders a roadmap of now, next and later.
